identity.title: Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech (Cincinnati/FAST screen)

technique.how: Ask the patient to smile or show teeth and look for asymmetric facial movement; have them close eyes and hold both arms out palms-up for 10 seconds, watching for one arm drifting down; ask them to repeat a simple sentence and listen for slurring, wrong words, or inability to speak. Any one abnormal item is a positive screen.
technique.prerequisites: Patient awake enough to follow simple commands; check a fingerstick glucose alongside the screen. Note time last known well.
technique.contraindications: None; if the patient cannot cooperate, observe spontaneous facial symmetry and limb movement instead.

interpretation.positive_finding: Any new facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech; in patients with neurologically relevant symptoms this raises the probability of stroke (pooled LR about 5.5).
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of all three findings lowers but does not exclude stroke (LR about 0.4); posterior-circulation strokes, which often present with dizziness or ataxia, are commonly missed by this screen (Kothari: 66% sensitivity overall vs 88% for anterior circulation).
interpretation.pitfalls: Bell palsy, old deficits, intoxication, hypoglycemia and seizure mimics all produce false positives; isolated vertigo, ataxia, visual field loss and neglect are not captured, so a negative screen must not stop a stroke work-up in a dizzy patient.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: activate stroke pathway/immediate imaging and time-critical reperfusion assessment. Negative: lowers probability but still image if dizziness, ataxia or visual symptoms.

estimates.target_condition: Acute stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) among patients with neurologically relevant symptoms
estimates.population: Pooled studies of patients with suspected stroke evaluated with modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
estimates.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and relevant laboratory tests
estimates.quote: LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1 ... LR of 0 findings = 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25-0.61

estimates.target_condition: Stroke or TIA (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal, scored by physician)
estimates.population: Convenience sample of 171 ED and neurology inpatients, 49 with stroke/TIA
estimates.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke or TIA
estimates.quote: abnormality in any 1 of the 3 stroke scale items had a sensitivity of 66% and specificity of 87% in identifying a stroke patient.

estimates.target_condition: Anterior circulation stroke (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal)
estimates.population: Same 171-patient convenience sample; subgroup with anterior circulation stroke
estimates.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke, anterior circulation
estimates.quote: The sensitivity was 88% for identification of patients with anterior circulation strokes.

sources.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.

Zhelev Z, Walker G, Henschke N, Fridhandler J, Yip S. Prehospital stroke scales as screening tools for early identification of stroke and transient ischemic attack. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019;4:CD011427.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative screen to exclude posterior-circulation stroke in a patient with acute dizziness, ataxia, diplopia or visual field loss; use HINTS/gait assessment and imaging pathways instead.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Any positive item with symptom onset within the reperfusion window is a time-critical emergency; do not delay activation for a glucose result unless hypoglycemia is confirmed and deficits resolve with correction.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Kothari 1999: excellent reproducibility between paramedics/EMTs and physicians for total score (ICC 0.89-0.92); facial droop was the least reliable item (ICC 0.75-0.78). Goldstein 2005: reliability of individual neurological findings ranges from slight to almost perfect, improved by standardized scales.

extraction_notes: Pooled LRs taken from Goldstein & Simel 2005 RCE abstract (Data Synthesis); the JAMA table itself was not viewable, so location is the abstract. Kothari 1999 sens/spec are physician-scored, from the abstract; LRs computed from the reported sens/spec (no CIs reported). The 2019 Cochrane review (source 2) did not pool CPSS because of heterogeneity and high risk of bias; it is cited for context only (CPSS had the highest sensitivity in the field but lower specificity than MASS/ROSIER) and carries no estimate here. Estimates are kept separate for the anterior-circulation subgroup rather than averaged.
